activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves.
story:
The town hall meeting was packed by the time Quinn found a seat beside Victoria, three rows from the front. On the table lay a stack of poster boards, and the first one showed a magnified picture of a microbe floating in a droplet of water. A man at the microphone was saying the town's well water was unsafe, and then he pointed at Ms. Lin, who ran the water testing lab, and said, "I accuse her of hiding the results." Ms. Lin stood up, folded her arms, and said, "I plead the Fifth."

Half the room murmured. Victoria leaned over and whispered, "What does that even mean?" Quinn had wondered the same thing two weeks ago, on a Sunday, when a detective on a TV show said the exact same words and refused to answer a question. Quinn had looked it up that night instead of doing math homework. The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves. So saying those words meant Ms. Lin didn't have to answer if her answer might make her look guilty of a crime.

At the front, the council chair asked Ms. Lin to sit down while they sorted things out. A woman near the front held up a raffle ticket and complained that the prize money from last month's fundraiser had been paid partly in counterfeit bills, and that only someone on the counting committee could have swapped them. She wanted every committee member questioned right then, out loud, in front of everyone.

Quinn thought about that. If the committee members answered one by one, each answer would be a kind of test, and one wrong word could make someone look guilty even if they weren't. She raised her hand, and when the chair nodded at her, she stood. "They can't make them answer," she said. "It's the Fifth Amendment. Nobody has to be a witness against themselves in a criminal case. That's what Ms. Lin meant." The chair looked at her for a long moment, then turned to the woman. "The committee will submit to proper questioning through the county office, not through a show of hands here."

Victoria nudged Quinn's elbow. "You knew that off the top of your head?" "Watched a lot of detective shows," Quinn said, and sat back down. Ms. Lin caught her eye from across the room and raised one hand, palm out, in a silent thank you. The chair banged the gavel and moved on to the well water vote.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A symbol is an object, person or event that stands for an idea beyond itself, and a reader must support any meaning they give it with details from the story.
story:
The bus jolted over the pothole by the greenhouse, and Alexa's binder slid off her knees and spilled across the sticky floor. She gathered the pages while Charles-Antoine leaned over the seat in front of her, holding his copy of the short story like it owed him money.

"Ms. Wardak wants a paragraph on symbolism by tomorrow," he said. "I don't even know what that is."

"An object that stands for an idea bigger than itself," Alexa said, reading off her notes. She'd copied it down fast at the end of class, when Ms. Wardak had assigned the story about the old woman and the red door. "Like the door in this story. The narrator keeps mentioning it. Page two, page five, again near the end."

"So it means danger," Charles-Antoine said. "Red means danger. Done. Can I demolish this discussion now and go back to my music?"

"You can't just say that," said Jovan, sliding into the seat beside Alexa. He tapped the page with two fingers. "You have to prove it from the text. Ms. Wardak took points off my last essay for exactly that. She wrote 'support your claim' three times in the margin. In red pen."

Alexa looked at the story again. The red door appeared the first time in a paragraph about the woman's late husband, who had painted it the spring before he died. Then the granddaughter refused to touch the door. Then, in the last line, the woman opened it herself. Alexa frowned. Danger didn't fit. Nothing bad came through that door. What came through it was morning light, and the smell of the garden her husband had planted.

"It's not danger," she said slowly. "It's him. The door is a symbol for everything she lost, and opening it at the end means she's deciding to keep living anyway." She read the lines aloud, and Jovan nodded, and even Charles-Antoine pulled one earbud out.

"Optimistic reading," he admitted. "Show me the husband part again."

The bus rattled past the glass shop downtown, and the low sun hit a prism hanging in the window, throwing a stripe of colour across Alexa's page, right over the paragraph she was underlining. She copied the three quotations onto a fresh sheet: the painting, the granddaughter's refusal, the final opening. Three pieces of proof. Not a feeling, proof.

"There's foreshadowing too," Jovan said, pointing. "The cracked hinge in paragraph two. The door sticks, then it finally opens. That hints at the ending before it happens."

"That's cheating," Charles-Antoine said. "The author knew the ending the whole time."

"That's the whole job," Alexa said.

They passed the paper back and forth until the bus reached their stop. Jovan climbed down first, then Charles-Antoine, then Alexa, who realized halfway down the steps that she had left her favourite pen in the seat pocket, the silver one her grandmother had given her, and the bus was already pulling away, trailing diesel smoke and her one good pen and the whole warm argument behind it. She stood on the curb holding the proof.

"Tomorrow," Charles-Antoine called over his shoulder, "you're explaining my paragraph too."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true.
story:
The number 42 bus jolted over a pothole, and Joseph grabbed the pole as his phone buzzed again. Griffin had texted the same thing five times since Monday: the eighth-grade talent show was rigged, the judges had already picked a winner, and entering was pointless. Today's text read, "Everyone knows it. Even Meliane says so."

"Joseph! Over here." Meliane waved from the middle of the bus, backpack on the seat beside her. She scooted it onto her lap to make room, and Joseph dropped down, exhaling as the day let go of him a little.

"It's not true," she said before he could sit properly. "I never said the show was rigged. I said I was nervous about it."

"Griffin says you said."

Meliane's mouth tightened. "He's telling everyone that. I heard it from three people in gym, four at lunch. Nobody asked me first." She stared out the window at the laundromat sliding past. "And you know the worst part? This morning, standing at my locker, I almost believed it myself. Like, maybe I did say it and forgot?"

That was the strange part, Joseph thought. She had heard the rumor about herself so many times that it had started to sound true. It reminded him of the sneakers he'd wanted all summer. He'd never once checked whether they were actually better than his old ones; he'd just seen the ad so often that the claim had worn a groove in his brain. Every bus in the city carried that ad, the one with the famous sprinter grinning above the words "ordinary shoes are for ordinary people." He'd looked up from his phone one day and realized he could recite it. Nobody had proved anything about those shoes. He had just seen it five, ten, fifty times, and somewhere in there it had turned into a fact in his head.

"Can I see your phone?" he asked Meliane.

She handed it over. He scrolled through her messages, counting. "Four different people sent you the same rumor today. Four. And a fifth one told you out loud."

"So?"

"So think back. Before any of them texted you, did you believe the show was rigged?"

"No. Obviously not. I'm doing a piano piece."

"And has anyone shown you proof? A leaked email, a photo, anything?"

Meliane drummed her fingers on her knee. "No. Just people repeating it."

"Then that's the test." He held up her phone. "You believe a thing, or half believe it, and the only reason you can name is that you heard it five times. Take away the repeats, and there's nothing left. It's like that sprinter ad. Say a thing enough times and it starts feeling true whether it's true or not. That's all that's happening here."

The bus shuddered to an abrupt stop at Maple and Ninth, and Ms. Santos, the driver, called back, "Hold the rail, you two, this corner's rough." Joseph grabbed Meliane's sleeve without thinking, steadying her as the bus swung.

"Thanks," she said. Then she sat up straighter. "Okay. But Griffin isn't going to stop just because I say it's not true."

"No. But he'll stop if nobody repeats it." Joseph pulled out his phone and typed slowly, showing her the screen before sending. "Griffin. I asked five people for proof and got zero. Meliane is doing the piano piece. Stop forwarding it."

She watched the message fly off. "You didn't have to do that. You barely know Griffin."

"He texts me the same stuff. I'm kind of doing this for me too." Joseph felt a small twist of guilt; he'd forwarded one of those rumors himself, back on Tuesday, without checking anything.

At the front of the bus, Ms. Santos pulled the lever and the doors folded open for a woman with a stroller. Joseph stood and offered her his seat, then leaned back toward Meliane.

"Your piano piece," he said. "What are you playing?"

"Something fast. You should come hear it."

"I'll be there," he said, and rang the bell for his stop.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Practicing in several shorter sessions spread over days usually builds a skill better than the same total time crammed into one long session.
story:
Megan slid her flute case onto the music stand and flipped it open, but the gleaming keys seemed to smirk at her. For three straight lessons she had fumbled the same six measures of the solo Ms. Yilmaz assigned, and tomorrow was Friday, lesson day again. Kristen, unpacking her clarinet on the next chair, leaned over. "Same spot again?"

"Same spot," Megan groaned. "I practiced forever on Thursday night. Like two whole hours. And I still crashed on the trill."

Kristen frowned. "That's weird. Two hours should be plenty." She held up her reed to the light. "Unless the problem isn't how long you practice."

Megan stared at her. A memory surfaced, sharp as a popped balloon: last fall, before the spelling bee, she had crammed fifty words into one Sunday afternoon and then blanked on "parallel" at the microphone, while Alvin had studied his words a little bit every single day and taken home the trophy. Alvin had shrugged afterward and said, "Little bits, lots of days. That's my whole secret." She had thought he was just being modest, but now her instinct told her something was there. Maybe her flute worked the same way. She decided to devise a plan on the spot and test it. "I'm going to do twenty minutes a day, every day this week," she announced. "Same total time as my big Thursday night, but spread out."

"That's the opposite of your usual cram," Kristen said. "Subjective question, though. Is it going to be more boring?"

"Probably," Megan said. "I'm doing it anyway."

So Monday she played the six measures slowly, twenty minutes, timer ticking on the stand. Tuesday her fingers still stumbled, but only twice. Wednesday she added the trill, and it came out clean on the fifth try, which felt like fireworks going off in the music room. Thursday she played the whole passage three times in a row without a single crash, and she actually laughed out loud in her living room, scattering the cat. When Friday arrived, she marched into the music classroom practically bouncing, and when her turn came she lifted the flute and poured those six measures out smooth as water.

Ms. Yilmaz lowered her pencil. "Megan, that's the best I've ever heard you play that. What changed?"

Megan grinned across the room at Kristen. "I stopped saving it all for the night before. Twenty minutes a day beats two hours on Thursday, every time." She raised the flute again, ready for whatever came next. "Give me something harder."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Babies under one year should be put to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, blankets or toys, which lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
story:
Nathaniel had been at his cousin's house for exactly three days when Mr. Popal knocked on the door holding a baby carrier and a diaper bag. Mr. Popal lived next door, and he and his wife had a meeting they couldn't miss, and Nathaniel was the only person in the house old enough to be trusted with their daughter, Wren, for two whole hours. Nathaniel said yes before his aunt could even finish asking. His first real babysitting job. He could already picture telling Kaysen and River about it at school.

"Everything you need is in the note," Mr. Popal said, pinning an index card to the diaper bag. "Bottles are in the front pocket. We'll be back by eight." Then he was gone, and Nathaniel was alone with an eight-month-old, which felt like being handed the controls of a rocket.

For the first hour everything went great. Wren sat on a blanket on the living room floor and laughed while Nathaniel waved his arms like a conductor conducting an invisible orchestra of one very small fan. But around seven she started to fuss, then cry, then wail. Nathaniel tried to diagnose the problem the way he'd diagnose anything: hungry? He offered the bottle; she pushed it away. Wet? The note said check, so he checked; fine. Tired, then. He rocked her, walked her in circles past the kitchen twice, and slowly the crying wound down until her head drooped against his shoulder.

He carried her toward the portable crib his cousin's family kept in the spare room, where he'd already laid a soft, fluffy blanket and tucked a small stuffed rabbit in the corner. It looked cozy. It looked perfect. He was halfway through lowering her when his eye caught the index card still stuck to the bag, and he stopped. Safe sleep, the note said in Mrs. Popal's tidy printing. Babies under one year go to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface, with no pillows, no blankets, no toys. It lowers the risk of sudden infant death.

Nathaniel stood there with a sleeping baby on his chest and a fluffy blanket in the crib, and it hit him that it would have been naive to assume a soft crib meant a safe crib. His mom had said something like that once and he'd half-listened, but here it mattered. Carefully, holding his breath, he pulled the blanket out, lifted out the rabbit, and pressed his palm on the mattress. Firm and flat, just like the note said. He laid Wren down on her back, stepped away, and waited. She smacked her lips once and kept sleeping.

At eight o'clock sharp, Mr. Popal and his wife came through the door, whispering. "Is she down?" Mrs. Popal mouthed, and Nathaniel nodded, leading them to the spare room like a museum guide unveiling a masterpiece. She peered into the bare crib, at the empty mattress, at her daughter flat on her back, and put a hand over her mouth. "Nathaniel," she whispered, "we left that note for our niece last month, and she ignored every word of it." Mr. Popal gave him a thumbs-up and whispered, "Same time next Thursday?"

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Answering an insult with another insult tends to escalate a situation, while a short, calm statement like "That's not funny, stop" gives nothing new to fight about.
story:
Ryder sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open, watching Kelly-Ann's face on the screen. She held up a cue card she had made, with six words printed in thick marker: THAT'S NOT FUNNY, STOP.

"Say it like you mean it," she said. "Not like you're reading a cereal box."

He tried it. "That's not funny, stop."

"Better. Now say it to me like I just mocked somebody."

Ryder's mind slid back to Tuesday, to the lockers outside the gym. Edward had been doing an impression of the new kid's stutter, drawing a small crowd, and Ryder had fired off a spontaneous comeback about Edward's haircut. It was clever. Everyone laughed. For about ten seconds Edward looked embarrassed, and then he turned it into a game, doing the stutter louder, wilder, and suddenly the new kid was carrying his books down the hallway alone with his head down. Ryder remembered thinking, right there, that his joke had handed Edward more material instead of shutting anything down. A clever insult gives the other person something new to fight about. A short, calm statement gives them nothing.

That was the pattern Ryder had worked out on the bus home, testing it against everything he could remember. Every time somebody answered an insult with another insult, things got louder and worse. Every time someone just said stop, flat and quiet, the whole thing seemed to lose fuel. He didn't know exactly why it worked. He only knew it did.

"Kelly-Ann, what if it doesn't work on Edward?" he asked now. "He feeds off attention."

"Then you've given him attention he can't use," she said. "One line. No comebacks. If you start trading insults, you're playing his game on his board."

Ryder had to admit his bias against Edward had made things easier in a way. It was simple to decide Edward was just mean and leave it there. It was harder to think about what to actually do. So he and Kelly-Ann rehearsed all evening, until Ryder could say the line without his voice cracking, and he made her promise not to jump in and rescue him tomorrow. He wanted to extract a real promise from her, not a polite maybe.

The next morning Edward was at the lockers again, doing the stutter. Ryder's heart slammed, but he kept his voice level. "That's not funny, stop."

Edward blinked. He opened his mouth, closed it, and shoved his hands in his pockets. The crowd drifted off with nothing to watch.

After gym, though, Edward caught Ryder at the water fountain. "That kid," Edward said, staring at the floor. "Marcus. He lent me his bus fare my first week here, before I knew anybody. Didn't even ask for it back." He rubbed the back of his neck. "I didn't know it was him at first, with the stutter. Then I did."

"So why keep doing it?" Ryder asked.

Edward shrugged, then looked at the empty hallway. "Want to walk to the bus stop with us? Both of us?"

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The equality rights in section 15 of the Canadian Charter came into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws.
story:
Samantha stood in the marble hallway of city hall with her cue cards sweating in her hand. In twenty minutes, Mr. Popal's class would take turns at the Charter Day display, and each student had to read one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and then explain it, in their own words, to whoever stopped to listen. She had drawn section 15, equality rights, and she'd practiced until her little brother could recite it.

Gwendolyn leaned over the display case, her nose an inch from the glass. "Why does your section have a different date printed beside it?" she asked. "Mine just says 1982."

Samantha looked. Next to section 15, in small type, was 1985. Every other section on the poster said 1982. Why would one right start three years late? she wondered. Rights didn't seem like the kind of thing you could postpone, like a dentist appointment.

"That's weird," Giovanni said over her shoulder. "Maybe it's a typo."

"It's printed twice," Samantha said. Once on the poster and once in the booklet chained to the display stand. Same number, 1985. She flipped the booklet to the back and found the answer in a footnote so short she read it three times to be sure. The equality rights in section 15 had come into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws.

She sat down on the cold marble steps to think it through. So the words existed in 1982, but they weren't law yet. It was like a rule posted on a gym door that didn't count until Friday. Why would a government need extra time? She turned the pages of her booklet and noticed how many old laws there were, hundreds of them, and how many would have to be checked against a new promise of equality. That would take a while. It wasn't that anyone was against equality, she decided. It was that changing rules takes work.

"There you are," Gwendolyn said, plopping down beside her. "Mr. Popal says you're first."

Samantha's stomach did a slow flip. She imagined the whole crowd, imagined herself freezing, imagined the embarrassment of standing silent in front of a microphone. Then she tried something. In her head she simulated the moment: she would walk up, unfold her cards, and if her voice shook, it would still carry the words. The words were solid. They had survived since 1982, or 1985, depending on the section.

When her turn came, she read the section aloud, then set the cards down. "In my own words," she said, "it means everybody gets equal benefit and protection of the law, no matter who they are. And here's the part I didn't know this morning. This section didn't actually start until 1985, three years after the rest of the Charter, because governments needed time to fix their laws first."

A woman in the front row, holding a citizenship pamphlet, raised her hand like a student. "So my equality rights are younger than I am," she said.

"By a lot," said Samantha. "The Charter's mostly a contemporary of my parents, but this part is closer to my age."

Gwendolyn whispered, "You sounded like you'd known that forever."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: The Jewish afterlife is often called olam ha-ba, meaning the world to come, though the phrase itself does not appear in the Hebrew Bible.
story:
Tristan had been to the cemetery twice in his life before Saturday, and both times had been for people he barely knew. This time it was for his grandfather, and he carried the small notebook his grandfather had left him, a frugal man who had written everything down for sixty years, from grocery prices to the names of birds. In the back of the notebook, on a page of his own, Tristan had written his problem: for Mr. Vargas's class he had to compare how two religions explain what happens after death, and he only knew one side, his own.

He was standing near the tent when he noticed a boy from his science class, Adrien, standing under an umbrella two rows over, at a different graveside. After both services thinned out, the boys ended up walking the same path toward the gate, and Tristan, who was not usually brave, said the first true thing that came to him. "I don't actually know what your side believes. About after. I have to write about it and I don't want to get it wrong from a website."

Adrien considered this, steering around a puddle deep enough to submerge the whole toe of a shoe. "We went to my great-uncle's shiva in the spring, and my grandma kept saying this phrase. Olam ha-ba. It means the world to come." He paused. "That's the Jewish afterlife, mostly. But here's the weird part. I asked my dad where it says that in the Torah, and he said the phrase itself isn't actually in the Hebrew Bible at all."

Tristan stopped walking. "It's not in the book? Then how does everyone know it?" The idea snagged in him the way a loose thread snags. If the words weren't written anywhere in the scripture, then the belief had traveled some other way, mouth to ear, generation to generation, like his grandfather's bird names. He said, "Wait here," and went back to the tent, where his uncle was collecting the flower stands, and borrowed the worn Bible that had rested on the coffin during the service. It was a Christian Bible, but the Hebrew scriptures were in the front of it, and Tristan figured that part would match.

He sat on the low stone wall near the gate and did what his grandfather would have done, which was test the thing instead of trusting it. He could not read Hebrew, so he could not search the original, but he thought about it differently. The idea, not the exact letters, was what mattered. He remembered his minister saying heaven was "not described, only promised," and he realized both traditions might work the same way: the door is named, but nobody claims to have seen the room.

"I look like I have one working neuron, don't I," Adrien said, sitting down beside him with the umbrella tilted to cover them both, because it had started to drizzle again and Tristan had forgotten any coat. Tristan noticed and scooted closer so more of the umbrella caught him.

"It's the opposite of what I thought," Tristan said. "I thought the answers would be completely different. Yours has a name, the world to come, and mine has a name, heaven, and neither one is really drawn out anywhere. Both of them are more like a promise people carry than a place people describe." He wrote in the notebook, pressing hard enough that it would show through the thin page, because his grandfather had taught him that a frugal person uses both sides.

Mr. Vargas, who had come up the path with his collar turned against the rain, glanced at the notebook without reading it. "You two are the last ones here," he said, "and the gate locks at six." Tristan closed the book and stood, then held out the umbrella handle so Adrien could duck under it first as they walked toward the gate together. "You'll have to read me what you write," Adrien said. "After it's graded, I mean. My dad will want to know if you got it right."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
story:
Wyatt leaned over the boards at the far end of the rink, watching the zamboni crawl past in its slow, shining lap. On Saturday the regional coach would post the tournament roster, and Wyatt had one job before then: tell Rafaelle who he thought should take the last forward spot, Danny from his old league or Cole, the new kid everyone talked about.

"Both of them average a point a game," Rafaelle said, scrolling his phone in the bleachers. "Identical. Twelve games, twelve points. The coach says it's a coin flip, so he asked us."

They had been arguing about it since Tuesday. Cole had scored four goals in one game in November, and the story had run in the town paper with a headline calling him a rising star. Danny never made the paper. Wyatt remembered that about him from two years ago, back when they were linemates: steady, quiet, always in the right lane.

"Wait," Wyatt said. He grabbed a napkin from the snack bar and a pencil stub from his pocket. "Show me every game." Rafaelle read the numbers out loud while Wyatt wrote them in two rows. Danny's row looked like the heartbeat on a hospital monitor, even and calm: one point, one point, two points, one point, over and over. Cole's row jumped around like the monitor had gone haywire. Four goals in one game, then nothing for three games straight, then a hat trick, then two pointless weekends in a row where, according to the recaps, he had barely touched the puck.

"You can't exclude the games where he vanished," Rafaelle said. "They count the same as the four-goal game."

"That's the whole problem," Wyatt said. "The average treats them the same, but they're not the same." He tapped the napkin. "They both end up at one point per game, but one guy gets there steady and the other swings between great and terrible. The average doesn't tell you which is which."

Mr. Whitehead, the rink manager, stopped his cart beside them and glanced at the napkin. "That's the most sensible thing I've heard in this building all week," he said, and drove off toward the locker rooms before they could ask what he meant.

Rafaelle was quiet for a moment. "Remember when you picked Kellan for the playoff team last year because of his one huge game?"

"I try not to," Wyatt said, though of course he remembered it perfectly. Kellan had scored five in the semifinal and then taken a single shot in the final, and Wyatt had spent the whole car ride home wishing he could undo the choice. Maybe that was why he kept looking at Danny's even little row and feeling something like empathy for the players who never got headlines.

"I'm not saying Cole is bad," Wyatt said carefully. "I'm saying the number we were given hides the thing we actually need to know." Rafaelle pulled up his phone again, then lowered it, then pulled it up again, thumb hovering over the coach's contact.

"Two names, one spot," Rafaelle said. "You type it."

Wyatt took the phone, looked out at the fresh ice gleaming under the lights, and started typing.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The sprinkler valve in the corner of Natalie's backyard had a rusty handle, and every Saturday morning she cranked it open so the hose could fill the water balloons for drill practice. The whole team gathered on her lawn because Mr. Grant, the neighbor who coached them, said it was the flattest grass in the neighborhood. It was only week three of the season, and the team was new, thrown together from three different schools, and so far they had lost every game.

"All you did was hog the ball," Jocelyn said, pegging a balloon at Yassine. It burst against his shoulder and soaked his shirt.

"I was open," Yassine said. "Natalie, tell her I was open."

Natalie didn't answer. She was counting on her fingers, quietly, the way she did when a pattern was forming in her head. Week one, everyone had been polite and nervous and terrible. Week two, they had started arguing, and the arguing had not stopped. Even Mr. Grant had noticed, because he had started ending practice early and standing by the fence with his arms crossed, watching them like a man trying to decide whether their season was endangered.

That night she borrowed her older sister's psychology textbook and sat on the porch with a flashlight. She wasn't looking for anything in particular, but a page caught her eye. A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. She read it twice. Forming, when everyone is polite. Storming, when everyone fights. Norming, when the fighting settles into rules. Performing, when it finally clicks.

On Saturday she tested it. When Jassine and Jocelyn started up again about the last game, she stepped between them with a dripping balloon in each hand. "We're storming," she said. "That's the second stage. It's normal."

"The second stage of what?" Yassine asked, wringing out his sleeve.

"Tuckman's stages. Forming, storming, norming and performing. We're right on schedule." She tossed them each a balloon. "So the test is this. If it's a real pattern, we should stop fighting and start working together without anybody telling us to."

The test took longer than she expected. They argued through the balloon drills and through the next two losses. But in week five, Jocelyn passed to Yassine without being asked, and Yassine shouted "nice look" instead of complaining, and by the end of practice they had invented a hand signal, two taps on the shoulder, that meant switch. Nobody had called a meeting about it. The rules had just appeared, the way norms were supposed to.

The week after that, they won. Not by luck, either; they won because everything revolved around quick passes instead of one person, and because when Yassine got doubled, he tapped his shoulder and Jocelyn was already moving. After the final whistle, Mr. Grant walked over to the sideline with a slow smile.

Natalie turned the sprinkler valve to shut off the water and looked at her muddy, grinning teammates. "Stage four," she said. "Right on schedule."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: Compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest.
story:
The farmers' market smelled like peaches and kettle corn, but Theodore had brought math instead of money. His grandmother had given him fifty dollars for his birthday with one condition: he had to put it in a savings account and figure out what it would become. The bank table sat between the honey stand and a man selling memoirs about his years as a lighthouse keeper, and behind it, Mr. Tran was stacking pamphlets at a right angle to the table edge, perfectly perpendicular, like everything he did.

Theodore's problem was simple. Simple interest paid five percent on his fifty dollars every year, so that was two fifty a year, times five years, twelve fifty, sixty-two fifty total. He could do that in his head. But the second column on the pamphlet, the one labeled compound, kept coming out bigger, and he could not see why. Nobody was adding money. Nothing was changing. He'd added nothing, the account had added nothing, and yet the numbers grew apart a little more each year.

Esme was at the market too, buying corn with her father, and she drifted over when she saw Theodore frowning at the pamphlet. "What's wrong with it?" she asked. He showed her the two columns. She read them twice, then pulled a pencil from her bag. "Okay, cooperate with me here. Walk me through year one." Two fifty, he said. Year two, simple gives you another two fifty. Year three, another two fifty.

"Then why does compound say more than two fifty in year two?" Esme said. Theodore started to answer, then stopped. He looked at the numbers again. In year two, the compound column showed interest on fifty-two fifty, not fifty. In year three, interest on a bigger number still. "It's getting paid on the interest too," he said slowly. "Compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned. So the interest itself starts earning interest."

"Which one are you picking?" Esme asked. The compound account was the obvious answer, but there was a catch, and the catch was in the fine print: he couldn't touch the money for the full five years. Sixty-two fifty was within reach whenever he wanted it. The compound account would be bigger, but locked. He thought about the new fishing rod at the hardware store, the one he'd been circling since June.

Kenneth wandered by with a bag of apples and voted loudly for the rod. "You could have it by September," he said. "That's five years of not-having it versus one month of having it." Esme pointed out that in five years he'd be seventeen, and a rod bought now would be an old rod by then, and besides, fifty dollars locked away might teach him something the rod couldn't.

Mr. Tran watched the three of them argue over the pamphlet without saying a word. Finally Theodore slid the form across the table and checked the compound box. Mr. Tran stamped it and handed back the receipt, and Theodore folded it into his pocket, thin as a leaf, while Kenneth bit into an apple and the honey seller called out her prices behind them.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the staff line for the note G.
story:
Peyton had been staring at the same sheet music for twenty minutes, and every note still looked like a stranger. The trumpet rested on her knee in the practice room at the community center, and down the hall she could hear the beginner band already warming up for Thursday rehearsal.

"Why do you keep counting lines?" Aden asked from the doorway. He had his trombone case under one arm and a granola bar in his hand.

"Mr. Hoang told me to find G before I play anything, because our whole first song starts on G. But I keep landing on the wrong note, and every time I do, Aimee hears it, and I just can't face that humiliation again." Last week she had squawked through an entire measure while the clarinets snickered, and Mr. Hoang had asked her to stay after and try again, alone.

She traced her finger over the strange swirl at the start of the staff, the treble clef, following its curl with the tip of her pencil. Around and around it went, and then she noticed something. The swirl looped its way through the lines and wrapped itself around the second one, circling it like a ring around a finger. She counted from the bottom. First line, second line. She put her pencil dot on the second line and hummed the note she thought lived there, then pressed the trumpet's first and third valves.

A clear, round G came out.

"That's it," she said, almost dropping the pencil. "The clef circles the line for G. It's like it's pointing at it." She checked it three more times, starting from different spots on the staff, and each time the curl led her back to that same second line. "It even makes sense of the name. It's also called the G clef."

"That's the most trumpet sounds all month," Aden said, mouth full of granola. "You sound almost optimistic."

"Why shouldn't I be?" She stood up, straightened her music on the stand, and carried the trumpet toward the rehearsal room. Aimee was already in her seat with her flute.

"Find your G yet?" Aimee asked.

Peyton raised the trumpet. "The clef finds it for me." She took a breath, traced the swirl with her eyes one last time, and played the first line of the song, clean and steady, all the way to the end.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: In the United States, the national Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222, and it connects callers to a local poison control center at any hour.
story:
The family group chat lit up at 7:04 with Lydia's first post: "At the Hendersons'. Toddler is asleep, dog has been fed, I am basically a professional." Her dad replied with a thumbs-up, and Brinley, who had been added to the chat for emergency backup, sent three fire emojis. Lydia set her phone face-up on the counter and told herself she would prioritize the actual baby over the phone, which was exactly what Ms. Van Dijk had told her class last spring when she'd given the babysitting talk. She had taken notes. Somewhere.

The trouble started with a smell. It was faint and sharp and coming from the hallway, and it was not there one minute and very much there the next. Lydia followed it and found the toddler, awake after all, standing by the laundry room door with an open bottle of cleaner in both hands, the cap on the floor, a wet shine across her chin and one small hand. The toddler said, "Uh oh," which was somehow the worst part.

Lydia's mind went white, then sorted itself. She took the bottle, set it high on the shelf, and wiped the little girl's mouth and hand with a damp cloth, exactly as her notes had said. Had she swallowed any? Lydia hadn't seen, which meant she had to guess, and guessing was not good enough. She carried the toddler to the kitchen, and there, taped to the fridge at eye level, was a folded paper with a phone number written in thick marker: 1-800-222-1222. Under it, in smaller writing: Poison Help.

She called it, her thumb shaking only a little. A woman answered right away, even though it was past nine at night, and Lydia blurted out everything in the wrong order. The woman slowed her down. "You've reached your local poison control center," she said. "Tell me what the bottle says." Lydia read the label aloud, and the woman asked about the wet hand, the wiped chin, the timing. Then she walked Lydia through what to watch for and told her to call back at any hour if anything changed. "Even at three in the morning," she said. "That's what we're here for."

While the toddler drank water from a sippy cup and patted the dog like nothing had happened, Lydia sat on the kitchen floor and typed into the chat: "Baby might have licked cleaner. Called Poison Help. Poison control says she's fine, watch her, they're local and open all night." Then she added, "I found the number taped to the fridge." Brinley replied instantly: "WAIT there's a hotline?? sending this to my mom." Her dad wrote, "Calling you in five. Proud of you."

The rest of the night was tedious in the best possible way: two more rounds of pat-a-cake, one story about a rabbit, a symmetry of blocks stacked and knocked down and stacked again. When the parents came home at ten, Lydia had the paper from the fridge in her hand. "You should give this number to every sitter you ever hire," she said. "I'm putting it in my phone right now."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Beak size is inherited, so after the 1977 drought the survivors' offspring had larger beaks on average than the birds before the drought.
story:
Maria stared at the blank worksheet in Mr. Khan's classroom and felt like the paper was staring back. Question three wanted her to explain how the finches on one small island ended up with different beak shapes than the finches on the islands next door, and she had exactly nothing written down. The bell wouldn't ring for another twenty minutes.

"You could just copy my answer," Hailee whispered, sliding her paper an inch across the lab table. Maria shook her head. She wanted to actually understand it, not just survive it, because Mr. Khan had said the unit test would ask the same idea in a new way, and copying never helped her before.

At lunch she sat with Hailee and Addison near the window and pulled out her phone. Addison was scrolling through old family photos, laughing at one of Maria's dad in middle school. Maria looked at the picture, then at her own reflection in the dark screen, and frowned. "Wait," she said. "That's my nose. That's literally Dad's nose on his face and on mine." Addison squinted between the photo and Maria and agreed that it was strange and also kind of hilarious.

Maria stopped laughing halfway through her milk carton. If her nose came from her dad, then finch beaks came from finch parents. That part was easy. The hard part was why the beaks would change, since nobody was picking out bird noses. She wrote a message to her older cousin that night and read it twice before sending it: "You know the finches from science, the ones on the islands? I think the beak size gets passed down like how I got Dad's nose. But how would all the birds on an island end up different from the birds that were there before? Tell me if I'm wrong. Please don't just say ask Mr. Khan."

The reply came while she was brushing her teeth: "You're on the right track. There was a drought in 1977 on one of those islands. After it, the babies that hatched had larger beaks on average than the birds before the drought. Look up what happened to the survivors." Maria read it three times, then pulled her notes onto her bed and spread them out like a detective with evidence boards. Survivors, she thought. Survivors had survived something. The drought. The drought killed the plants that made the easy seeds, so the birds with small beaks had nothing they could fracture open, and the birds with bigger beaks could crack the harder seeds that were left. The survivors were the bigger-beaked birds. They were the parents. And since beak size was inherited, the babies were bigger-beaked than the generation before the drought, on average.

The next morning she found Hailee at the lockers. "Nobody changed the finches," Maria said. "The drought just picked who got to be a parent, and the parents passed their beaks down. That's why the islands ended up different." Mr. Khan was walking past with a stack of invasive species posters for the hallway, and he paused long enough to hear the last sentence. He raised his eyebrows at Maria and said he'd have to evaluate her reasoning on Friday's test. Maria grinned, because for once, that was exactly what she wanted.

"Question three," she told Hailee, holding up her worksheet. "Watch this."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phishing is a scam in which someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away passwords or other private information.
story:
The phone was warm in Arthur's pocket, still new enough that he kept touching it through his jeans. His mom had handed it over at the kiosk by the food court twenty minutes ago, and now she was three stores down, leaving him alone with it for the first time. Arthur slid onto a bench outside the pretzel stand, unwrapped the plastic, and started setting things up. Sylvie and Bryn found him there before he'd finished his first text.

"Let me see," Sylvie said, dropping her bags. "Ooh, it's the green one. Bryn, look."

Bryn leaned over Arthur's shoulder. "Download the game. The one with the dragons. My brother plays it nonstop."

Arthur created an account, chose a dragon, and lost his first battle in under a minute while his friends laughed. Then his phone buzzed. A text, from an address that claimed to be the game's official support line. YOUR ACCOUNT WILL BE DELETED IN 24 HOURS UNLESS YOU VERIFY YOUR PASSWORD. REPLY NOW.

"That's weird," Arthur said. "I just made the account. Why would they delete it already?"

Bryn squinted at the screen. "Probably a rule about new accounts. Just send the password, it says official right there."

Sylvie wasn't so sure. "My aunt got something like this last month. She called it phishing. That's when someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away your password or private stuff."

Arthur looked at the message again. Something didn't fit. If the company already had his password, why would they need him to send it? The question had a shape to it, like a math problem where one number refused to line up. He decided to test it. "I'll reply with something wrong," he said. "If they're real, they'll say it's incorrect. If they're fake, they'll take anything."

He typed gibberish and sent it. The reply came back instantly: THANK YOU, ACCOUNT VERIFIED. NO DELETION.

"They took it," Sylvie said. "They'd take garbage. It's fake."

His mom was still down the corridor, so Arthur stood up. He didn't want her to intervene and decide the phone was too much trouble on day one, but he knew she should see it. He walked fast, phone out, and found her at a shoe store. She read the texts twice, then blocked the number and reported it, showing him how. Her hands were careful and her mouth was a straight line.

"That was fast thinking," she said finally. "Most adults fall for that."

Arthur felt proud, and then something else underneath it. The phone in his hand was less simple than it had been an hour ago. It buzzed and chimed and pulled at him, and now it also carried things like this, patient strangers waiting for a mistake. His objective had been a dragon and a game with his friends, and already the world had found him through the glass.

He walked back to the bench. Bryn had unlocked the game and leveled up his dragon twice.

"Hey, that was mine to lose," Arthur said, holding out his hand for the phone.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The term 'active listening' was introduced by psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957; it means trying to understand the speaker's point of view, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words.
story:
Jayden stomped down Maple Street with a stack of flyers under his arm. Syed was supposed to help distribute them for the school gaming-club fundraiser, the one where every dollar of revenue went toward new controllers. Instead Syed had walked off with Milena to test the new claw machine outside the corner store, without a word.

Jayden had texted him twice. Nothing. That was the part that stung, he decided, shoving a flyer into the gate of the blue house. Not the claw machine. The silence.

Mr. Hosseini was watering his roses by the curb. "Big stack," he said. "Need a hand?"

"I'm fine." Jayden tried the next gate and it stuck.

"Slow down or you'll jam your fingers." Mr. Hosseini set down the hose. "You look like a kettle about to whistle."

Jayden exhaled. "My friend ditched me. Again. For the same person." He hadn't meant to say that much.

Mr. Hosseini picked up half the stack. "In my counseling course, they made us practice active listening. Rogers and Farson came up with that term back in 1957. Supposedly it means you try to understand the speaker's point of view, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words." He handed a flyer to a jogger, then added, "Hardest thing I ever learned. I'm still bad at it."

Jayden worked down his side of the street. Repeat the meaning back? It sounded like something from a poster in the guidance office. But the rule stuck in his head like gum on a shoe, and by the time he reached the corner store, he had a plan.

Syed was alone at the claw machine, slumped, out of quarters. He saw Jayden and straightened too fast.

"You're angry," Syed said.

"Don't do that. That's not what I said." Jayden planted himself in front of the machine. "I said I felt like you picked her over me. Three times now. That's what I said."

Syed blinked. His shoulders came down an inch. "So you felt I picked her over you? Like she matters more?"

"Yeah. That."

"I didn't know it looked like that. She's just fun to beat at claw machines. You're my best friend. Since second grade." Syed kicked the machine's leg, lightly. "I'm bad at saying stuff out loud."

"Me too." Jayden sorted his flyers and held out half the stack. "We still have four blocks."

They distributed the rest of the street together, racing porch to porch, and when the last flyer was gone Syed pulled two quarters from his pocket and held them up.

"One claw attempt," he said. "You steer, I work the button."

Jayden grabbed the joystick.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Instant replay was first used in a live sports broadcast by CBS director Tony Verna during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963.
story:
The whistle blew just as the ball crossed the line, and forty thousand people in the stadium screamed at once, because nobody could tell whether Felix's uncle had caught it cleanly or trapped it against the turf. On the giant screen, the play appeared again, frozen, then sliding forward frame by frame like a slow beetle. Felix leaned forward in his seat, squished between his dad and Cadence, and felt his heart hammer against the thin fabric of his team jersey.

"Watch the ball," Cadence said, gripping his sleeve. "Watch it, watch it."

The replay showed it clearly. The uncle's fingers slid under the leather a heartbeat before it touched the ground. The crowd roared all over again, the sound contagious, spreading from section to section until even the vendors were shouting. Down on the field, the referee spread his arms, and the scoreboard lit up with the word TOUCHDOWN.

Felix's dad laughed and shook his head. "You know, when I was your age, my grandfather told me they couldn't do that. Replay. Television couldn't show you a play again while the game was still going."

"That's impossible," Felix said, though even as he said it he was thinking hard. How would anyone argue about a call? How would fans at home even know what happened?

"Swear on my sandwich," his dad said. "It took somebody clever to figure it out. A CBS director, during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963. Tony Verna. First time instant replay ever ran on a live sports broadcast."

Felix filed that away like a ticket stub, because right now there was a more urgent problem. The stadium had announced a halftime contest: one kid from each section would be picked to catch a punt on the field, and Felix wanted it more than he had ever wanted anything. The catch was, you had to prove you belonged to your section, and his ticket had gone through the wash in his jacket pocket. The paper was a pale gray rag now, its ink smeared into a模糊 blur.

Halftime was nine minutes away. The sweepstakes people were already walking the rows, handing out wristbands to anyone who could show a seat number. Felix negotiated fast with the woman in the aisle, offering his jersey number, his row, anything. She shook her head and moved on.

"Wait," Felix said suddenly. He grabbed Cadence's arm. "The screen. The screen shows everything here. During warmups it showed the crowd, section by section. If they replay it, we'll be in it, sitting right here, and the seat numbers are painted on the rail." It was a guess about something he couldn't see directly, the same way the replay had settled what nobody's eyes had caught live. But if the pattern held, it would work.

He ran down to the rail and waved both arms at the camera operator, who was panning the crowd between plays. The operator grinned, zoomed in, and there on the giant screen, crisp and enormous, sat Felix and Cadence and his dad, directly beneath the stenciled number for Section 14, Row F. The woman in the aisle checked her tablet, looked up, and snapped a green wristband around Felix's wrist.

The teams jogged off, the valve of the halftime air cannon hissed open, and T-shirts rained down around them like confetti. Cadence shrieked and lunged for one. Felix stood there, wristband gleaming, staring at the empty green field where he was about to run. "Nine minutes," he said. "Nine minutes and I'm down there."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
story:
The gym smelled like popcorn and floor wax, and Nevaeh had spread her notebook across two seats so she could keep the shot chart for the Rockets while she worked. The school paper had agreed to run her ranking column, but only if she could explain how the numbers were built, and she was still stuck on that part. Every basket, every miss, every free throw went into her tallies, and by the fourth quarter the page looked like a swarm of tiny marks.

"Who cares about all that?" Ruben said, dropping into the seat beside her with a cup of something tropical from the concession stand, the kind that dyed his tongue orange. "Just put whoever scores the most at the top. It's obvious."

"It's not obvious," Nevaeh said. She turned the notebook toward him. "Deshawn scored fourteen tonight, but he took twenty-two shots. Amara scored twelve and took nine. Who was better?" Ruben squinted at the marks like they were a foreign language, and Linda leaned over from the row behind them, chewing her straw.

"That's like that baseball thing my cousin showed me," Linda said. "David Justice and Derek Jeter. In 1995 Justice had the higher batting average, and in 1996 Justice had the higher average again. Both years, he beat Jeter."

"So Justice was better," Ruben said.

"That's what's weird," Linda said. "You add the two seasons together, and Jeter's average is higher. Justice wins each year and loses the whole thing." Nevaeh stopped writing. Somewhere under the buzzer and the squeak of sneakers, a question formed, the kind she liked, the kind that itched. How could that even work? She pulled out her phone and found the numbers, then stared at them while a Rockets free throw clanged off the rim.

"Wait," she said. "I want to test something." She drew two columns in the margin and started stacking tally marks beside each, glancing between the screen and the paper. The pattern she saw made her sit up straight. "It's like my shot chart. If you blend everything together, the mixture doesn't have to match any single piece." She looked at the court, where the scoreboard said one number for the whole game even though a hundred little things had made it. "One number is hiding a hundred events."

The buzzer ended the game and Ms. Nwosu came up the bleacher steps, whistle still around her neck, collecting the stat sheets. "How's the column coming?" she asked. Nevaeh told her the whole problem, Justice and Jeter, the shot charts, the strange flip when the seasons were combined, and said she wanted the paper to print two seasons side by side instead of one ranking, and that she was drafting a petition to get full box scores announced at halftime instead of just points scored.

"Because a single number can lie," she said.

Ms. Nwosu smiled and tapped the notebook. "Then show them the marks."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Relationship researcher John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which is about one specific action, from criticism, which attacks a person's character with words like 'you always' or 'you never'.
story:
Andrew stared at the family group chat on his phone, thumb hovering over the keyboard. In the chat, his mom had asked why he was sulking at dinner, and his sister had typed "DRAMA" with three eye-roll emojis, which was annoying but not wrong. He and Eden had blown up at each other in the cafeteria on Friday, and now it was Sunday night, which meant he had less than twenty-four hours before he had to sit two seats away from her in first period.

He typed a draft to Eden anyway, even though she'd blocked his texts. He pasted it into the family chat by mistake, then deleted it fast before anyone could read it. The draft said, "You never keep anything private. You always spill my stuff to everyone."

His dad replied from the couch ten feet away: "Whatever that was, maybe finish typing it somewhere I can't see it."

Andrew flopped onto his bed. He kept replaying Friday, the way Eden had laughed when she told Colin that Andrew had cried during the movie they saw over spring break. It wasn't even a secret, exactly, but it felt like one, and her telling it felt like proof of something bigger. That was the part he couldn't stop chewing on. Was Eden actually a leaky, untrustworthy person, or had she just done one dumb thing?

Last semester, Mr. Yilmaz had made them read an article about a researcher named John Gottman for health class. Andrew remembered it now because Mr. Yilmaz had made them highlight it, which at the time seemed pointless. He dug the photocopy out of his binder. The researcher distinguished a complaint, which was about one specific action, from criticism, which attacked a person's character with words like "you always" or "you never." Andrew read the sentence twice. His draft message was pure criticism, and he hadn't even noticed himself writing it.

He tried a rewrite. "You told Colin I cried at the movie on Friday. That embarrassed me." No always, no never. Just Friday. It looked smaller on the screen, which was strange, because it also felt more true. He couldn't text Eden directly, so he opened the shared doc where they planned their history project, due Monday morning at 8 a.m., and typed it as a comment at the top of page three, where she'd actually see it.

Monday morning, Eden slid into her seat and turned around before the bell. "I didn't think it was a big deal," she said, arms crossed, chin up, defiant. "Colin asked why you were quiet that night."

"I know. It still stung," Andrew said. "You told him on Friday. That's all I'm saying happened."

Eden's shoulders came down an inch. "Okay. That's fair. I shouldn't have told him." She pulled out her laptop. "We still have the conclusion to integrate into the doc before class starts."

They wrote side by side, shoulders almost touching, and when the bell rang, Eden nudged his elbow and said, "Next movie, I keep my mouth shut, I promise."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is thinned with water while wet, but once it dries it becomes water-resistant, so brushes must be washed before the paint dries on them.
story:
Nathan spread his brushes across Grandpa's porch table and felt his stomach drop. Every single one was stiff as a stick. He and Gage had left them in the garage overnight after painting the wooden birdhouse for Grandpa's birthday, and now the bristles wouldn't bend at all.

"We ruined them," Gage said, poking one. It clattered against the table like a tiny drumstick.

Nathan picked up a brush and turned it over, thinking. The paint had been slippery and wet yesterday. He'd even added water to a dab of blue to make it thinner for the sky, and it had spread like a dream. So why couldn't they just add water now? He held the stiff brush under the outdoor tap and scrubbed. Nothing. The dried paint held on like glue.

"Acrylic washes out while it's wet," Nathan said slowly, "but once it dries, water won't touch it. That's why the brush got ruined. We were supposed to rinse them before the paint dried." He said it like a discovery, because it was one. He'd never thought about it before, and now the proof was in his hand, hard as a pencil.

"So all we had to do was wash them last night," Gage groaned. "Great."

"But wait." Nathan's mind was racing ahead, the way it did when a problem flipped into an idea. "If dried acrylic won't let water through, then the birdhouse is sealed. Waterproof. We painted three whole coats yesterday." He grabbed Gage's sleeve. "Don't you get it? It can go outside in the rain. Grandpa can hang it by the feeder and it won't wash off."

They were still arguing happily about where to hang it when Layton biked up the driveway, waving something over his head. "You left this at my house!" It was Grandpa's old notebook, the one he called his memoir, full of stories about the farm where he grew up. Layton had borrowed it to read about the summer of the runaway goat. Nathan flipped through the pages and stopped. Tucked between two chapters was a folded drawing of a birdhouse, in pencil, with shaky, careful lines.

"That's Grandpa's design," Nathan whispered. "The exact one we made. Same roof, same round hole." They hadn't copied it. They'd never even seen it. They had just liked the same shape, the same little perch, the same sloping roof.

When Grandpa came out to supervise the hanging, they handed him the notebook first. He read the drawing, then looked up at the painted birdhouse gleaming in the sun, its blue roof already proof against any rain.

"Well," he said, and his voice went thick, "it's not counterfeit. It's the real thing."

Nathan climbed the ladder and hammered in the hook.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet; 'most students at our school walk to school' could be tested with a survey.
story:
The sign on the library table read GROUP PROJECT, and Prisha had already claimed the seat closest to the window. She slid a notebook across to Madison and tapped a line she had written in purple pen: "Most students at our school walk to school." "I put it in our poster," Prisha said. "It's true. I think."

Madison read it twice. "Is it, though? Or is that just what you believe?" Behind them, a man in the biography section was reading aloud to two kids about a famous orchestra conductor, and Madison's mind snagged on the word the way it always did, but she pulled it back to the poster.

"It's not an opinion," Prisha said, sitting up straighter. "I didn't say walking is better. I said most people do it. That's different." Asia, who had been shelving returns for her volunteer hour, drifted over and looked at the line. "Has anyone counted, though?" she asked. Madison chewed her pencil. "That's the thing. Nobody has. Ms. Brown's class did lunch preferences last year, but not this." Prisha tried to evade the question by changing the subject to poster colors, but Madison put a hand flat on the notebook. "It could be checked. Even if nobody checked it yet. We could survey the whole school. Homerooms, one question, how did you get here today."

They took the idea to the librarian at the front desk and asked to borrow the clipboard. She raised an eyebrow, printed fifty blank tally sheets, and said the survey sheets could live in the returns bin until Friday. On Friday, Madison counted the columns three times at the corner table while Prisha held the sheets flat and Asia made check marks on a fresh page. Buses won. Walkers came in second, cars third, and two kids wrote "scooter" with a doodle of a helmet.

"So I was wrong," Prisha said. She didn't sound upset, only surprised, the way you are when a door opens from the side you didn't push. "But the sentence was still the right kind of sentence. We just needed the count." They rewrote the poster in the library's meeting room, and when the class voted on which project to hang in the hallway, the vote was unanimous. Prisha drew a small bus at the bottom, with every window filled in.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Line dances, in which a group repeats the same set of steps facing the same direction, let people dance together without needing a partner.
story:
Alexis stood in front of the bathroom mirror with his tie draped around his neck like a snake that had given up. The dance started at seven, and it was already five thirty, and he still didn't know how he was going to survive it. Everyone else had partners or groups or at least a plan. He had a tie and a problem.

"Mom, why do they even call it a dance if nobody actually dances?" he called down the hall. She didn't answer, which meant she was on the phone with a colleague about work, which meant he was on his own.

He flopped onto his bed and texted Bodhi. Bodhi had gone to the winter dance last year, so Bodhi knew things. Alexis drafted the message three times before he settled on "how do you dance when you don't have anyone to dance with." It sounded less pathetic than "everyone will stare at me and I will stand by the punch table until I turn into a plant."

The reply came fast, which meant Bodhi was pacing his room too. "Line dance," Bodhi wrote. Alexis stared at the words. He remembered the summer barbecue at his grandfather's old neighborhood, when Mr. Wiśniewski from next door had jumped up mid-burger and joined a row of people on the grass, all of them stomping and clapping and turning the same way at the same time like a giant accordion made of humans. Nobody had asked anybody to dance. Nobody had held anybody's hand. They had just folded themselves into the line.

Alexis sat up so fast his phone slid off the blanket. He called Daniyal. "Okay, tell me everything about the line dance at the last one."

Daniyal laughed, but not in a mean way, in an excited way, which was Daniyal's whole personality. "It's the best part. Everybody does the same set of steps, and everybody's facing the same direction, so you don't need a partner. You just find the line and jump in. It's like six steps and then they repeat forever."

"Six steps." Alexis grabbed a notebook from his desk and wrote SIX STEPS at the top. "Which six?"

" Grapevine right, grapevine left, stomp, clap, that thing where you bounce, then turn a quarter." Daniyal's voice got muffled, like he was demonstrating into his sleeve. "Watch, I'll show you, but you can't laugh at my socks."

They spent the next twenty minutes with their cameras propped against stacks of books, shuffling across their respective bedrooms. Alexis turned the wrong way twice and knocked his knee on his desk once, but by the third run-through his feet had started to know the pattern without him. It was almost logical, he thought: one direction, one set of steps, repeated. You couldn't be wrong alone when everyone was doing the same wrong thing with you.

At seven ten, the gym was hot and loud and bright, and Alexis stood at the edge of the floor with his heart going like a drum line. The opening song ended and the DJ said the words he'd been waiting for. The floor split into lines, everyone facing the stage, and a gap opened up near Bodhi and Daniyal. Alexis walked out, planted himself in the gap, and waited for the first stomp.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Research on children at overnight camps has found that most campers feel at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stays mild.
story:
Alexa laid her sleeping bag across her bed like a body and stared at it, wondering how four weeks at Camp Wyoka could fit inside one duffel bag when it barely fit inside her head. The camp rules prohibited phones, which meant no texting her mom, no checking in, nothing but letters that took three days to arrive. Three days. She imagined a wave of missing home hitting her on night two with no way to call out, and the thought sat in her stomach like a swallowed stone.

Amina arrived at noon with a roll of duct tape and a bag of sour candies, and they started labeling things. "You're quiet," Amina said, smoothing tape over a water bottle. "You've been quiet since Tuesday."

"I keep thinking about homesickness," Alexa admitted. "What if I'm the only one? Everyone else will be doing canoe races and I'll be the weird kid crying at lights-out." Saying it out loud made the guilt worse, because her mom had already paid, and had that hopeful face on, and Alexa felt like she was planning to ruin the whole thing.

Then she had an idea. Trystan had gone to the same camp last summer, and he lived two houses down. She knocked on his door with the question already formed, because a person who'd actually been there was better evidence than a feeling. "Did kids get homesick at Wyoka?" she asked. "Like, actually?"

Trystan leaned against his doorframe. "Research on overnight camps says almost everybody misses home at least a little. It's like the most normal thing there." He grinned. "For most of them it stays mild, too. Nobody had to leave. My whole cabin talked about it the first night, like a roll call. Then it mostly just faded into the schedule."

Alexa walked home slowly, turning that over. She had assumed homesickness was rare, a flaw, but if nearly every camper felt at least a flicker of it, then it wasn't a personal defect; it was closer to a rule, like how yawning was contagious in a crowded room. And if it stayed mild for most kids, then the pattern suggested something else: it wore down on its own, the way a new school did. She still couldn't see Camp Wyoka from her bedroom, but she could see the math, and the math was friendly.

Back upstairs, Amina had sorted the duffel into piles and was holding up two flashlights. "Headlamp or the red one?" she asked.

Alexa took the headlamp, clipped it to the front pocket, and zipped the bag shut in one firm pull. "Both," she said. "We're going in prepared."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a string at its exact midpoint halves the length that vibrates, and the note rises by one octave.
story:
Jonathan had been practicing in his grandfather's garage every afternoon for a week, and every afternoon the same thing went wrong. He would tune the guitar, play the open E string, and then press down at the twelfth fret, and the note would come out sour instead of matching.

Meliane sat on an overturned milk crate, eating leftover noodles from a container. "You're pressing too hard," she said. "My cousin does that."

"No, it's not pressure." Jonathan played the open string again, listening. The garage smelled like motor oil and old cardboard, and a spider had built a web in the window corner that nobody wanted to disturb. "Watch this." He pressed the twelfth fret and plucked. The sour note buzzed through the quiet.

Baby, who lived next door and had wandered in as he always did, leaned against the workbench. "Sounds like a dying goose," he said cheerfully.

"Thanks." Jonathan laid the guitar flat on his lap and studied the neck. He knew the twelfth fret was supposed to give him the same note, one octave higher. That part he had learned from a poster at the music shop, and it made a strange kind of sense to him: the string was pressed exactly at its halfway point, so only half the length vibrated. Half the string, one octave up. He measured with his eyes, fret by fret, from the nut to the bridge. Something was off, and it was something he couldn't see directly.

"The string's too old," Meliane suggested.

"That would make it dull, not sharp." He tested the idea. If the fret sat in the wrong place, then the note would be wrong by the same amount every single time, and the errors would pile up, cumulative, as he climbed the neck. So he checked the fifth fret against the next string, then the seventh, then the ninth. The lower notes matched almost perfectly. The trouble only appeared near the top.

"The bridge," he said suddenly. He turned the guitar over. The bridge had shifted, just barely, toward the bass side, loose enough to slide when the strings were tightened. That was the hidden cause. He borrowed his grandfather's small screwdriver from the pegboard and nudged the bridge back until the twelfth fret note landed true, the same as the open string, only higher.

"Play the dying goose again," Baby said.

Jonathan played a slow scale up the neck. Every note rang clean. "That refutes the dying goose theory," he said, and Meliane laughed so hard she nearly dropped her noodles.

They stayed until the light through the window turned orange. Baby asked if Jonathan could play something for the neighborhood party where his mother was cooking Thai cuisine, and Jonathan said he could try, now that the guitar agreed with him.

"Half a string, one octave," Meliane said, plucking the twelfth fret herself. "Weird."

"Yeah," Jonathan said. "But it works."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach, causing the "butterflies" feeling.
story:
"Are you sure you don't want to wear the blue dress?" Mya's mom had texted the family group chat for the third time, attaching a photo of the dress hanging on Mya's closet door. Mya typed back "the green one" and muted the chat, because Grandma would chime in next with eleven exclamation points, and her stomach was already doing enough flip-flops for one evening. The dance started in an hour, and a small, loud part of her kept saying she could still fake a headache.

Tiana arrived at seven sharp, holding two hair ties and a plan. "Emery's going," she said, in the tone of someone stating a fact she intended to enforce. "You're dancing with him at least once, even if it's one random slow song in the middle. That's the whole mission." Mya said maybe, which in Tiana's language meant yes, and finished zipping the green dress.

In the car, Mya's little brother sat wedged between them on the way to his friend's house first. He stared out the window and said his stomach felt weird and his heart was going really fast, and he hadn't even done anything yet. Mya almost told him to stop making things up, but then she noticed he wasn't joking. She'd read something in Ms. Gallagher's class about how nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach and causes that exact flip-flopping feeling. She'd thought it was boring then. Now she looked at her brother's pale face and thought it might be the most useful thing she'd ever learned.

"You're not sick," she told him. "You're nervous, and your body released adrenaline. It makes your heart race and pulls blood away from your stomach. That's the butterflies." He frowned. "Then it's a false signal?" "It's real, it's just not a stomach bug," she said, and made him breathe slowly with her until they reached his friend's driveway. By the time he climbed out, his color was back, and he even waved instead of slouching.

Mya sat quietly for the last few blocks, testing the idea on herself. Her own stomach was still twisting, but if that was just adrenaline and racing blood, then nothing was actually wrong with her either. She checked the family group chat: Mom had texted a thumbs-up, Grandma had sent eleven exclamation points on schedule. She typed "going in" and put the phone away.

Tiana grabbed her hand at the gym doors, where the music thumped and Emery was already visible near the punch table, pretending not to look over. "One slow song," Tiana whispered. Mya took a breath, felt her heart hammering, and recognized it for what it was. Then she walked in anyway.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
story:
Nathan stood in the snack aisle gripping his list, which said, in his mother's handwriting, "usual granola bars." The tag under the usual granola bars read $7.49. Last month it had been $4.99. He checked the tag twice, flipped it over, and even looked behind it, as if a cheaper price might be hiding there.

Jolie appeared beside him with a basket on her hip. "Seven forty-nine? Did they dip them in gold?"

"There has to be a mistake." Nathan scanned the shelf. "Or a reason. Stores don't just add three dollars for fun."
