"They kind of do."

He didn't believe that. Stores were run by people who counted things, and people who counted things had reasons. He walked the aisle slowly, reading tags like a detective. The fancy yogurt in the cooler had gone up too, and so had the almond crackers. But the store-brand crackers, two shelves down, were the same price as always, and the shelf was packed so full the rows looked like cargo stacked in a ship.

"Interesting," Nathan said.

"That's a weird thing to say about crackers."

"Look. Everything that got expensive is half gone. Everything that's still cheap is stacked to the ceiling." He pointed at the oat bars, a different brand, doing the same job as granola bars, sitting fat and plentiful at $3.29. "I think when a price goes up, everybody just... switches. They buy the other thing. The substitute."

Jolie picked up a box of oat bars. "Substitute. Like a substitute teacher, but for snacks."

"Exactly. It does the same job." Nathan tested the idea by watching people. A man in a yellow jacket glanced at the granola price, made a face like he'd bitten a lemon, and dropped two boxes of oat bars into his cart. A woman with two kids did the same thing, twice as fast, because the kids were chanting for snacks in voices that shattered the tranquil hum of the store.

"It's happening right now," Nathan whispered. "Watch. Price up, everyone runs to the substitute. The substitute gets popular."

"Popular and still cheap," Jolie said. "For now."

At the checkout, Mr. Banerjee from next door was ahead of them, unloading his cart. Nathan spotted six boxes of oat bars. "Mr. Banerjee, did you switch from the granola ones?"

"The granola ones went up three dollars," Mr. Banerjee said. "The oat ones do the same job. My wallet voted." He laughed at his own joke so hard the cashier looked up.

Nathan bought four boxes of oat bars with his mother's money and exact instructions broken. At home he set them on the counter, and when his mother frowned, he held up the receipt like a trophy.

"Half the price," he said. "And I still have change."

She turned the box over, read the label, and bit into one.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away; this is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Maeva finished her first soccer practice of the season feeling great. She had sprinted until her lungs burned, taken a hard tackle from Greyson, and walked home through the park with her cleats swinging from one hand. "That wasn't so bad," she told Hussein at the water fountain. "I was worried I'd be too sore to move after sitting out all winter."

Hussein laughed. "Just wait two days." He was a veteran of the league, three seasons in, and he said it the way people say things they've learned the hard way. Maeva didn't believe him. Her legs felt fine, strong even, and she figured soreness was like sunburn: it showed up right away or not at all.

The next morning she was still fine, and she smirked about it on the bus. Then day two arrived. She woke up, swung her legs out of bed, and let out a yelp that brought her dad running. Her thighs burned like someone had wrung them out. She had to lower herself onto the toilet seat with both hands on the counter, and the stairs at school turned into a slow, sideways shuffle. Greyson clutched his own legs and groaned in sympathy at lunch. "Mine started this morning," he said. "I thought I'd dodged it."

Hussein slid his tray over. "It's called delayed onset muscle soreness," he said. "Hits 24 to 72 hours after, not right away. New or hard exercise, that's what does it." He shrugged. "Nobody told me my first season either."

Maeva turned that over all through math class. If the soreness peaked later instead of right away, then feeling fine after practice told you nothing about the real cost. Which meant Coach had been smart to make Saturday an easy recovery session, and it also meant something else, something about the tryout she'd skipped last fall. She'd told herself she was too tired that day, but maybe she'd just never pushed hard enough to know what tired meant. She couldn't go back and check. The choice was already made, and she still wasn't sure whether it had been caution or something closer to quitting.

There was a game on Saturday, and she intended to be there. On Friday evening she tested her idea in the park near her house. If the soreness followed its own schedule, easing off today wouldn't necessarily make it vanish by tomorrow, but it might keep it from getting worse. So she did one slow lap, easy jog, no sprints, and stopped while her legs still felt like legs. Her dad watched from a bench, arms crossed. "Hussein's family swears leg cramps are hereditary," he called out. "His uncle, his grandmother, apparently everybody." Maeva waved that off. This wasn't cramps, and it wasn't inherited. This was her own body keeping score.

Saturday morning she stood at the midfield line, thighs still aching but bearable, and bounced on her toes to feel it out. The referee raised the whistle. Greyson looked over from the far sideline and shouted, "Stairs still killing you?" Maeva grinned and shook her head once. Then the whistle blew.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Saying 'I'm sorry if you were upset' is often called a non-apology, because it expresses regret about the other person's feelings rather than about what the speaker did.
story:
The text from Haley glowed on Juliette's phone screen: "sorry if you got upset at lunch." Juliette read it aloud to Kamden, who was sprawled on his bedroom floor rebuilding a model bridge, toothpicks everywhere.

"That sounds like it's my fault for being upset," Kamden said, not looking up. "Like you're sorry I have feelings." He pushed a toothpick into place. "It's not sorry for what you did. It's sorry I felt a way about it."

Juliette stared at the words. She had meant them kindly. But reading them again through that lens, the way Kamden did, she saw it: the sentence never said she was sorry for spilling the secret about Haley's tryout solo. It only said sorry "if" Haley got upset. The "if" made the whole thing conditional, like maybe Haley had imagined the whole day.

"Is there a name for that?" she asked.

"Mr. Côté called it a non-apology last year," Kamden said. "He said half the apologies in movies are non-apologies."

Juliette set the phone down on the carpet. She thought about lunch, the way Haley's face had gone stiff when Priya mentioned the solo, the way Juliette had laughed and said, "Yeah, she's been practicing that one forever." She could still hear the sound of Haley's tray scraping back from the table.

She tried to paraphrase her own text into something true. "I'm sorry I told Priya about your solo. That was your news to share, not mine." She said it out loud to the toothpick bridge. It felt heavier than the text, like it cost something.

"Just send that," Kamden said. "Actual words. Not the immune version where nothing touches you."

Juliette typed it with her thumbs, deleted "I think," because that was another escape door, and typed it again. Before she could lose her nerve, she pressed send. The phone sat silent for so long that Kamden handed her a toothpick and put her to work on the suspension cables.

The bridge was half a tower tall when the phone buzzed. "Come over?" Haley had written. "I have the solo memorized. You're the only one who's heard it."

Juliette pulled on her jacket at the door. "Tell your mom I'm eating at Haley's," she called back to Kamden, and she was already down the front steps.

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: Erosion is the wearing away and carrying off of rock and soil; deposition is the dropping of that material somewhere else.
story:
Ms. Hosseini had built a stream table in the corner of the science room, a long plastic tray filled with packed sand and tilted on wooden blocks, with a hose that ran from the tap through a small brass valve. Romy stood in front of it with her notecards and nothing on them but a question mark.

"You go Thursday," Halle reminded her. "Same as the rest of us. You're not getting an extension."

"I know when I go." Romy turned the valve a quarter inch. Water slid down the tray and curled into the sand. Within a minute a channel had opened, a small canyon with steep little walls, exactly like the diagram of the Grand Canyon in the textbook. But something bothered her. She measured the channel with a ruler. Then she measured the pile of sand at the bottom end of the tray, where the water slowed and spread out.

"Where'd all this come from?" Koen leaned over her shoulder, fogging the glass of the window behind them so it condense into a grey film he drew a face in.

"It came from the canyon," Romy said. She checked the numbers again. "The channel lost exactly as much sand as the pile gained. Nothing vanished." She dug her finger into the pile. "The water carried it. That's the wearing away and carrying off part. Erosion." She pointed at the heap at the tray's end. "Then it dropped it here, because the water slowed down. Deposition. The dropping of the material somewhere else."

"So the canyon's just the hole where something used to be," Koen said.

"And the pile is where the something went." Romy turned the valve further, and Koen said, "Whoa, reckless," as the flood collapsed a sand wall and dumped half the canyon into the delta in three seconds. She shut the valve and stared at the wreckage.

"It still balances," she said quietly. She measured again, and it did.

On Thursday she stood at the front while Ms. Hosseini opened the tap. Romy turned the valve herself, one careful quarter inch, and let the class watch a river begin its work. "Millions of years at this speed," she said, "and you'd get something you could hike into. Watch the bottom of the tray." The first grains of sand tumbled loose, rode the current, and settled at the far end in a tiny, brand-new beach.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these versions are called isotopes, but they always have the same number of protons.
story:
Owen pressed his museum worksheet against the glass case and frowned at the little square marked C. Six, the square said, in a corner above the word carbon. Somewhere behind him, Hareem was already two exhibits ahead, and the first one to finish all ten elements won the extra planetarium ticket Ms. Tang had promised.

"How do you even know what that number means?" Kyra asked, catching up with her pencil clicking.

"It counts the protons," Owen said. He had figured that out at the second exhibit, where a brass plate explained that the small number on every square was the atomic number. Each element had its own, and the protons were what made it that element. He checked carbon again. Six protons. He wrote it down, feeling the paper go soft under his sweaty palm.

Then he reached the case with the skeleton of a horse and a label about carbon-14, and his pencil stopped. Carbon-14. But fourteen did not match six. His stomach dropped, because if the second number was also protons, then he had gotten every answer wrong, and Hareem was going to win by default. He stared until the words blurred. Maybe the plate at the start had said something about neutrons. He turned around and jogged back through the echoey hall, past the humming model of a volcano, the smell of dust and machine oil warm in his nose.

Kyra followed him and read the plate out loud over his shoulder. "Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. These versions are called isotopes."

"Isotopes," Owen repeated, and the whole thing snapped into place like a latch. Carbon-14 still had six protons, because six was carbon, always. The extra stuff was neutrons, and neutrons were the factor that could change without changing what the element was. He could not see a single proton or neutron, not through the glass or anywhere, but the numbers on the table let him quantify them anyway, which felt almost like a superpower. He ran the test in his head: hydrogen with one proton and hydrogen with an extra neutron would both still be hydrogen. It worked. He turned to Kyra, grinning so hard it hurt.

"Write this down before I forget," he said, and she did, in her durable gray notebook with the bent spiral, while Hareem's voice rang out from three cases away, asking if anybody had found element ten yet.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Placing onion cells in salty water draws water out of them, so the cell membrane shrinks away from the cell wall and can be seen; this is called plasmolysis.
story:
Juliette set the microscope on the kitchen table and peeled a paper-thin layer from the inside of an onion, the layer so translucent she could read the cereal box through it. Her worksheet had three empty boxes: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. So far she had found one of them.

"Is that the wall or the membrane?" Maina asked, leaning over her shoulder. Maina had biked over with the salt shaker from her own kitchen, because Juliette's mom had used all theirs for the pickles.

"That's the wall," Juliette said, tracing the brick-like outline with her pencil. "The straight edges. But the membrane is supposed to be right against it, and I can't see any line between them." She turned the fine focus one more revolution, and the image sharpened, but still there was just the wall and a smooth gray inside. No membrane, no dark dot for a nucleus. She squinted. "How can something be there and be invisible?"

Maina tapped the worksheet. "Ms. Ba said our grade comes from labeling all three."

Juliette sat back and remembered fourth grade, when she'd been sure her snowflake had melted before she could draw it. Her grandfather had shown her that if she caught it on dark wool instead of her warm glove, it lasted long enough to see. Sometimes you had to change the thing around the thing you wanted. She chewed her pencil. The cells were full of water. What if she changed the water?

"Onion cells are sitting in water," she said slowly. "What if the water isn't plain anymore?"

Maina held up the salt shaker. "You want me to?"

"One drop. At the edge of the cover slip."

Maina sprinkled salt into a spoon of tap water, stirred, and let a single drop touch the slide. Juliette watched through the eyepiece, hardly breathing. For a moment nothing happened. Then, like a curtain being pulled back, the inside of each cell shrank. A thin skin peeled away from the wall and crinkled inward, and there, unmistakable, was the membrane. Inside the shrunken skin, a small dark circle appeared: the nucleus, which had been pressed flat against everything else before.

"Look, look!" Juliette yanked Maina down by the sleeve. "It's pulling away from the wall! The membrane! And the nucleus!"

Maina stared. "The salt did that?"

"It drew the water out of the cells," Juliette said, already writing labels with her pencil, arrows pointing to the wall, the shrunken membrane, the dark nucleus. She flipped her notebook over and found the word printed at the bottom of the chapter she'd skimmed. "It's called plasmolysis."

"Sounds like a superpower," Maina said.

Juliette tilted the lamp, and the light refracted through the drop on the slide, throwing a wobbling rainbow across the table. She leaned down to the eyepiece again, grinning.

"Salt shaker," she said, holding out her hand. "One more drop."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A thesis can preview the argument by naming its supporting points in the same order the body paragraphs will discuss them.
story:
Emile had planned to spend Saturday at his grandfather's kitchen table anyway, because Grandpa kept a tin of lemon biscuits within reach of anyone who sat there, and because the essay was due Monday. The prompt was simple: should the school cut funding for the robotics team to save the music program? His class had argued about it for two days, which was longer than anyone had argued about anything except whether the cafeteria pizza counted as pizza.

He spread out his notes next to the biscuit tin. At the top of the page he had written a thesis, the sentence that was supposed to hold the whole essay up, and under it, three points: robotics costs more, music serves more students, and the school promised both programs last year. He had circled it all in blue pen the way Mr. Mendoza had shown them, and now he sat looking at it while the kitchen radio fluctuated between a weather report and something in a language he didn't recognize.

Timothe had texted him a photo of his own outline, and Charles had sent four texts, none of them about the essay. The last one said, "did u even start." Emile typed back "obviously" and turned his phone face down, because obviously was a strong word for one circled sentence and a biscuit.

Then he noticed something. His second point, music serving more students, was the argument he actually cared about, so he had moved it first in his outline, then felt bad for the cost argument and moved it up too. Now the outline read music, costs, promise. But his thesis still said the team cost too much, that music reached more students, and that the school had made a promise. The two lists didn't match. He read the thesis aloud to the empty kitchen. "It's like a menu that lists the courses in a different order than they're served," he said, and Grandpa, passing through with a watering can, said, "At my restaurant we served the soup whenever the customer asked for it," which was not helpful but was probably true.

Emile fixed the thesis so it named the points in the same order his paragraphs would discuss them: music first, costs second, promise last. Then he tested it. He wrote the paragraph topics in the margins of his outline, one word each, and checked them against the thesis like a man matching socks. Music, music. Costs, costs. Promise, promise. He did it twice, because the first time felt too easy, and things that felt too easy in Mr. Mendoza's class usually meant he'd missed something.

He sent Timothe a photo of the corrected page with the message "your thesis has to list your points in the same order you're going to argue them." Timothe replied with a single thumbs up, which Emile chose to interpret as gratitude. The fatigue in his right hand from all the circling was starting to feel like a real injury, and the cost argument still seemed kind of trivial compared to two hundred kids losing their orchestra, but the structure held. He straightened the pages, took one more biscuit, and started writing the first body paragraph, music first, exactly as promised.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: When a variable appears on both sides, as in 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, subtracting 3x from both sides gathers the variable on one side: 2x + 2 = 10.
story:
Keira stared at the practice sheet on the kitchen table. If she got every problem right tonight, her mother would let her go to Kaleigh's movie marathon on Friday. If she missed even one, she stayed home. The last problem on the page looked like a trap: 5x + 2 = 3x + 10. The x was on both sides, like a cat sitting in two doorways at once, refusing to pick a room.

She pulled out her phone and typed a message to Kaleigh. "The quiz is Monday and I still don't get the ones with x on both sides. Which x am I supposed to move first?" While she waited, she made a quesadilla and ate it too fast, the molten cheese burning the roof of her mouth, so she sat there fanning her mouth with the edge of her napkin and thinking about the problem instead.

Kaleigh's reply came in three bubbles. The first one said, "idk, I got that one wrong." The second disclosed something Keira hadn't known: "Harlyn says she moved the wrong one on purpose and still got the right answer. Ms. Müller just wrote 'ok' on it." Keira read that twice. Moving the wrong x on purpose? How could wrong still lead to right?

She set her pencil down and tried it. First she subtracted 3x from both sides, because 3x was the smaller one and somehow that felt polite. On the left, 5x minus 3x left 2x, and the 2 stayed put, so 2x + 2 = 10. She wrote that down. Then she subtracted 2 from both sides, and divided, and got x = 4. She checked it: 5 times 4 plus 2 was 22, and 3 times 4 plus 10 was 22 too. She actually said "ha" out loud, alone in the kitchen.

Then she tested Kaleigh's claim. She crossed out her neat work and started over, this time subtracting 5x from both sides instead. The left side became just 2. The right side became 10 minus 2x, so 2 = 10 - 2x. It looked worse, like she'd wrecked it, but she kept going, subtracting 10 from both sides and getting negative numbers that eventually turned themselves around, and there it was again: x = 4. Both roads, same answer. She flipped to the front of her sheet and did the same experiment on an easier problem, just to be sure the pattern held.

She texted Kaleigh one more message before bed. "You can move either x. I tried it both ways and got 4 both times. It's like both doors lead to the same room." Then she wrote out the whole last problem one final time, clean and slow, in her best handwriting.

The next morning her mother checked the sheet at the counter, problem by problem, while Keira buttered her toast. When she reached the last one she paused, then slid the page back across the counter with a small amendment to the deal: movie marathon, plus Kaleigh's house for dinner afterward, if Keira showed Ms. Müller the double-check trick on Monday. Keira grinned, folded the sheet into her binder, and zipped it shut.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
The gym was so cold that Livia called it the tundra, and she wasn't entirely joking, because she could see her breath near the water fountain by the doors. She pulled her sweatshirt tighter and found a spot on the bench beside Terrance, who had a pencil behind his ear and a folded piece of paper on his knee.

"Keeping stats again?" she asked.

"Somebody has to," Terrance said. "The box scores in the paper never name anyone but the starters." He drew a grid with careful lines, frugal with the space because it was his last clean sheet of paper.

On the court, Serenity was warming up, bouncing once, twice, then letting a shot fly. It rattled in. From the bleachers behind them, a girl named Priya's little sister stood on the third row and shouted, "My sister is the best shooter on this team! She's one hundred percent this season!"

Livia turned around. "One hundred percent of what?"

"Of her shots," the girl said, as if that settled everything. "She never misses."

Terrance flipped back a page in his notebook. "She took one shot," he said. "First game. It went in."

Livia thought about that all through the first quarter. One shot, one make. The number was true, and yet it felt like a trick. If Priya had missed that single shot, she'd be at zero percent, and nobody would be shouting anything. The percentage wasn't telling them much about Priya at all. She watched Serenity take six shots, sink three, and miss three, and Terrance marked every one, and fifty percent started to feel like a sturdier fact, because it rested on something.

At halftime, Livia wandered down to the fence behind the bench. Priya was sitting at the end of it, still in her warm-up jacket.

"Your sister says you're a perfect shooter," Livia said.

"I know." Priya grinned. "One for one. Can't argue with the math."

"Sure I can," Livia said. "One shot is like one raindrop deciding whether it's a rainy day." She pointed at Serenity, who was practicing free throws, calmly dropping in five of eight. "She's at fifty today, but she took real shots. Somebody tried to thwart her with that stat already, you know. Terrance read it out loud."

Priya's grin faded into something more thoughtful. "So if I never shoot again, I stay perfect forever."

"You stay perfect and useless," Livia said. "The number only means something if you feed it."

Priya chewed on that, then stood up and jogged to the scorer's table to check in for the second half. Livia went back to her seat and told Terrance to keep his pencil ready.

It took four minutes. The ball swung around the arc, and Priya caught it at the elbow, hesitated, and launched. It clanked off the back rim, and her little sister in the bleachers made a sound like a deflating balloon. Priya, though, laughed, held up one finger to the crowd as if to say, that's one data point, and got back on defense.

The next possession she caught the ball in the same spot and shot without hesitating. It dropped through clean, and Terrance wrote something down with great ceremony.

"What's her percentage now?" Livia asked.

"Fifty," he said. "The most honest number she's had all year."

"Perfect is overrated anyway," Priya called from the court. "I'm going for a hundred attempts."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Clothes left crumpled in a dryer or basket after the cycle ends tend to wrinkle as they cool, so taking them out promptly and folding them helps keep them smooth.
story:
The community room at the back of the bank had two washers, a dryer, and a long folding table, and Mr. Ho let the entrepreneurship club use it on Saturdays. Noemie was in charge of laundry day, which meant forty club t-shirts had to be clean, folded, and ready to sell at the farmers' market on Sunday morning. She had never done a full load on her own before, so she stood in front of the table with Jayson and Cameron and a heap of shirts on either side of her.

"Darks over here, lights over there," she said, sorting. "Mr. Ho said the red ones run the first few washes, so they get their own load." Cameron held up a grey shirt. "Grey's a dark," Noemie decided, and he tossed it over. Jayson wrote the price tags. They loaded the first batch, and while the washer drum thumped, the three of them packed jars of the nutritious trail mix the club was selling alongside the shirts. Mr. Ho leaned in the doorway and said the club account was doing well, and if the market went the way last month's had, their little business would flourish by spring.

The trouble started with the dryer. Noemie's older brother had come by earlier and asked them to wash his one good shirt for his bank interview, the interview at this very branch, at nine the next morning. His washer was broken and he had to work until closing. Noemie had said yes without thinking twice. But when the dryer buzzed, Cameron was elbow-deep in trail mix and Jayson was arguing about whether to raise the price of a large shirt to twelve dollars, and the shirts stayed in the drum, heaped and steaming, while the three of them counted the cash box and packed the car. By the time Noemie remembered, the load was cold.

She pulled out her brother's shirt and her stomach dropped. Creases ran across it in deep lines, sharp enough to look deliberate. A few club shirts from the same load were just as bad, but a stack she had pulled out early and folded flat was smooth. She laid her brother's shirt beside a folded one on the table and stared. "These were in the same load," she said. "The only difference is I got these out right away." Jayson frowned. "So they wrinkle while they're sitting there?"

"As they cool," Noemie said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "Left crumpled in there after the cycle ends, they wrinkle as they cool. Take them out promptly and fold them, they stay smooth." Cameron groaned, because it was nearly six and the bank locked its community room overnight. Noemie looked at the dryer's control panel, then at the clock. One more cycle. She rewashed the creased shirts, and this time she made Jayson stand beside the dryer with a timer while she and Cameron kept folding table space clear. The moment the buzzer went off, she pulled everything out piece by piece, snapped each shirt flat, folded it, and stacked it. Her brother's shirt came out last, and it cooled smooth and straight on the table under her palm.

Sunday morning her brother wore it to his nine o'clock interview, and Noemie watched him cross the lobby of the bank beside a row of neatly folded shirts in club bins. When he came out at half past, he walked straight to the community room and pointed at his own collar. "Not a crease on it," he said. "You're doing my laundry forever."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In written dialogue, a new paragraph begins each time a different character starts speaking, so readers can tell who is talking.
story:
Everly had been trying to write a story in her grandmother's back room all afternoon, and the notebook page was still almost barren except for one dense paragraph where her hero and the old lighthouse keeper argued about a storm. When Kim arrived for the sleepover, Everly shoved the notebook across the table. "Read this part and tell me if it works."

Kim squinted at the page. "Okay, so the keeper says the boat can't leave, and then he says the storm's too close, and then he says the radio's dead. Wait, who said the radio's dead? Was that him or the hero?" She flipped the notebook upside down, as if the answer might fall out of it. "I'm lost. Who is talking?"

Everly leaned over the page. Every line of speech sat in the same long paragraph, jammed together with commas and quotation marks, and she could see why Kim couldn't tell the voices apart. "I hypothesize that the problem isn't the words," she said slowly. "It's the shape. All the talking is stuck in one blob."

To test the idea, she copied the scene onto a fresh page, but this time she broke it apart. Every time the hero finished a line and the keeper began, she pressed return and started a new paragraph. She kept the ratio of narration to speech about the same, half description and half talking, so the only change was where the paragraphs fell.

"Now read it," she said.

Kim read aloud, and her voice swung back and forth without stumbling once. "The hero says go. Then a new paragraph, and it's the keeper saying no. It's obvious who's talking, because a new paragraph begins every time a different character starts speaking. Why didn't you do that before?"

"Because I didn't know it mattered." Everly laughed and grabbed the pen again. "Okay, that fixes who's talking. Now the other problem is that nothing big happens at the end. Mr. Rossi says a short story needs a clear climax, and mine just... trails off."

Kim tapped the window, where rain had started to hammer the glass. "Make the storm actually hit. Make the keeper choose between the radio and the boat."

Everly wrote fast, one speaker per paragraph, and when she finished the last line, the keeper shouting into the wind, she slid the notebook back across the table.

Kim read it in silence, then looked up. "Read me the next one tomorrow."

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: In Spanish, the simple future adds an ending to the whole infinitive, so "hablar" (to speak) becomes "hablaré," meaning "I will speak."
story:
Arthur stared at the blank line where his paragraph was supposed to be. Mr. Zhu wanted five sentences in Spanish about plans for next year, and it was due at the end of class. Twenty minutes left.

He knew his plans easily enough. He would join the track team. He would write to his pen pal, Mateo, in Madrid. He would speak Spanish every day, or at least try. The trouble was the verbs. Every time he wrote a plan, the sentence fell apart on the ending.

He wrote "hablar con Mateo" and frowned. That meant "to speak with Mateo," not "I will speak." He chopped the word down to "habl" and stared at the scraps, as if the missing piece might fall out of his pencil. Nothing came.

"Stop grinding your eraser," Yahya said from the next desk. "You're going to wear a hole in the paper."

"I can't figure out the future," Arthur said. He kept his voice low, because Mr. Zhu was walking between the rows and the room was supposed to be quiet. "I need I will speak. In Spanish."

Yahya leaned over and looked at Arthur's sentence. Then he flipped back a page in his own notebook, where he had copied a model paragraph off the board. His eyes went from his page to Arthur's and back, twice, like he was checking a pattern.

"You're cutting it up," Yahya whispered. "Don't. Look at how I wrote estudiar for next year. I wrote estudiaré. The whole infinitive stays, and the ending goes on the end. So for yours, hablar becomes hablaré."

"Hablaré," Arthur repeated under his tongue. He wrote it, then "hablaré con Mateo cada día." It looked longer than he expected, but whole. He tried the next one. "Correré en el equipo de atletismo." Then "estudiaré mucho." His pencil moved faster now, agile on the page, and the sentences stacked up like dominoes that finally stood.

At home that night he prolonged his practice, writing three extra sentences past the assigned five, because Mateo deserved a real letter and not a sad little paragraph. When his mother asked why he was still at the kitchen table, he said he had a friend in Madrid who would notice if he quit halfway.

The next morning he slid the paper onto Mr. Zhu's desk. Mr. Zhu read it, raised one eyebrow, and drew a small arrow beside the last sentence.

"Read this one to me," he said.

Arthur looked down at the line he had written without checking. "Viajaré a España," he said slowly. "I will travel to Spain."

Mr. Zhu set the paper down. "Ask your parents about summer," he said, and moved on to the next desk.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double with compound interest: divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate, so about 12 years at 6 percent.
story:
The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and coffee, and Isabelle gripped her birthday money, two hundred dollars, in a zippered bag because she did not trust her backpack pocket. Caylee and Arianna had come along for the walk, mostly for the free lollipops at the counter, but they crowded behind her at the desk where a woman in a navy blazer waited.

"Hi, I'm Ms. Asante," the woman said. "Opening a savings account?"

"Yes. But first I have a question." Isabelle unfolded the paper where she had worked everything out the night before. "Your sign says six percent interest. If I leave two hundred dollars for five years, simple or compound, which one gives me more?"

Ms. Asante's eyebrows went up, just a little. "Which do you think?"

"Compound. Because with simple, you only earn interest on the two hundred every year, over and over. With compound, the interest earns interest too." Isabelle traced her columns. "Simple gives me sixty dollars more after five years, so two hundred sixty. Compound gives a little more than that, like sixty-eight dollars. But I couldn't figure out when my money would actually double."

Arianna popped her lollipop out of her mouth. "Why double? You'll be rich by then anyway."

"Four hundred dollars is not rich," Caylee said.

Ms. Asante slid a printed sheet across the desk. It showed the same two columns Isabelle had made, simple and compound, and the compound number beat simple by exactly the gap she had guessed. But at the bottom was a line she had never seen: Rule of 72. Isabelle stared at it.

"What's the rule of 72?" she asked.

Ms. Asante smiled and tapped the words but said nothing else, the way a teacher does when she wants you to find it yourself. Isabelle muttered, "Seventy-two divided by something." She tried dividing by years. Then she divided 72 by 6, the percentage rate.

"Twelve," she said slowly. "Twelve years to double. I'm thirteen now, so I'd be twenty-five."

"That's the rule," Ms. Asante said. "Seventy-two divided by the yearly percentage rate. At six percent, about twelve years."

Arianna leaned over the counter. "Twenty-five is so old. You'll be, like, paying rent."

"You'd have four hundred dollars you didn't lift a finger for," Caylee said.

Isabelle pushed the bag of money across the desk. "Compound, please. I can persist with it. Twelve years is long, but I'm not spending it anyway."

Ms. Asante typed, and the machine hummed. "You know," she said, "some people think interest is a trick because they can't see it working. You built yourself a little algorithm on paper instead. That's more credible than most grown-ups who walk in here."

The printer clicked out a single blue receipt with a starting balance of two hundred dollars. Isabelle folded it into her pocket, next to her worn calculation sheet, and Caylee asked if there were any grape lollipops left.

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: After the very wet El Niño year of 1983 brought many small, soft seeds, selection on Daphne Major's medium ground finches reversed, favouring smaller beaks.
story:
Alyssa spread her notebook on the flat rock at the edge of the pond and weighted the pages with two pebbles, because the wind off the water kept flipping them. She had promised Denise and Harleen she would have the finch project figured out by Saturday, and Saturday was today. Her plan was simple: bring the girls to the pond, act out the birds, and see whether her idea about beaks even made sense.

"Bigger beaks are better," she said when they arrived, lugging a shoebox. "That's what I thought, anyway. Big beak, big advantage. So I devised a test." Inside the box were kitchen tongs, tweezers, and two bags of seeds, one holding large hard ones and one holding tiny soft ones. She pointed at the mud below the willows. "Tongs are big beaks. Tweezers are small beaks. We pick up seeds for thirty seconds each and count."

Denise took the tongs first, and Harleen called time from the bench. With the big hard seeds, the tongs crushed it. Alyssa's tweezers fumbled, dropping seed after seed, and the score was not even close. "Told you," Alyssa said, stacking her seeds in a little cattail-leaf cup.

Then Harleen said, "Wait, your notes say something weird." She turned the notebook toward the light. Alyssa leaned over and read the page out loud, slow, so it would stick. "After the very wet El Niño year of 1983 brought many small, soft seeds, selection on Daphne Major's medium ground finches reversed, favouring smaller beaks." Denise frowned. "Reversed? How can small be better?" Alyssa looked at the second bag of seeds and said, "Let's just try it."

They scattered the tiny soft seeds in the grass at the pond's edge. This time the tweezers darted and plucked, quick as anything, while the tongs knocked the little seeds around like an obstinate bull in a narrow doorway, gripping three at best out of every ten tries. Denise counted out loud from the bench, and when time was up she held up two piles: a heap of tweezers seeds and a sad pinch of tongs seeds. "Okay," she admitted. "Smaller beaks won. That's a total contradiction of round one."

"That's the point," Alyssa said. "It's not that one beak is better forever. It flips depending on the seeds. Big hard seeds, big beaks win. Then that rainy year came, 1983, and all those small soft seeds showed up, so on that island, Daphne Major, the medium ground finches with smaller beaks ended up doing better." She copied the numbers into her notebook, then underlined the year twice. Harleen was already scooping the leftover seeds toward the ducks, and one drake, unimpressed by anyone's beak, snatched the whole pile in a single gulp.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Hens lay eggs whether or not a rooster is present; without a rooster the eggs are unfertilized and cannot hatch into chicks.
story:
The field trip bus rattled up to the Henderson Heritage Farm, a historic site so old that the guide claimed the barn had stood since before the town had a name. Scarlett stepped off behind Zachery and Alexi, still holding the worksheet Ms. Villanueva had handed out, and the first thing she noticed was that the place smelled like wet straw and dust.

The guide split them into groups, and Scarlett's group got the chicken yard. Their job was to collect eggs from the nesting boxes and carry them in a basket to the farm kitchen, where a woman in a long apron would show them how people had cooked a hundred and fifty years ago. Zachery lifted a warm brown egg out of the straw and frowned at it.

"Will this hatch?" he asked. "If we put it back, could a chick come out?" He looked around the yard, counting the birds. "I don't see a rooster anywhere. Not one."

Alexi shrugged and kept gathering eggs, but Scarlett couldn't stop thinking about it. If the whole flock was hens, then where would chicks come from at all? On the bus, she had read one of the plaques by the gate, a faded sign about the farm's breeding flock, and it had said the farm kept a "notorious" rooster named Barnaby in a separate pen across the road, away from the visitors, because he chased people. She hadn't understood why that mattered until now.

"Wait," she said. "If the rooster is over there, and the hens are over here, then these eggs can't hatch. No rooster means no chicks. But the hens still lay eggs anyway, every day, whether he's here or not. So the eggs would just be eggs." She turned one over in her palm. "That's why the farm can collect them for cooking without stealing future chickens."

"That's a guess," Zachery said.

"Then let's test it." Scarlett carried the basket to the kitchen, where the aproned woman had set up an old lamp in a darkened corner. She showed them how farmers used to hold an egg up to the flame to see inside, a trick that worked best in a room with no windows. Scarlett lifted an egg toward the light. The shell glowed a plain, clear gold, empty of the shadowy veins a chick would have. She tried a second egg, then a third, and each one was the same.

"So none of these would ever be chicks," Zachery said slowly. "Not because they went cold, but because they never could be."

The woman in the apron nodded without saying anything more and slid the eggs into a bowl of flour. Outside, through the open door, Scarlett could see the far pen across the road, where a large bird with burning red feathers strutted along the fence, keeping his distance from everyone.

"There's Barnaby," she said, pointing. "Not even he can help those eggs now. They're already in the batter."

Zachery laughed and wiped his hands on his jeans. "Then I'm eating the evidence."
